p1.e: Every day shows a habit, so use Present Simple. She is third person singular, so add -s.

p1.q: Look! The students ____ in the garden now.
p1.e: Look! and now show an action happening now: Present Continuous, am/is/are + V-ing.
Since + a starting point with a situation that continues to now needs Present Perfect: have/has + V3.
Yesterday is a finished time, so use Past Simple (V2), not Present Perfect.

p1.q: When the teacher arrived, the students ____.
p1.e: The studying was already in progress when the teacher arrived: Past Continuous (was/were + V-ing).

p1.q: By the time I arrived, the class ____ already.
p1.e: Two past events: the earlier one uses Past Perfect (had + V3). By the time signals this.

p1.q: She is tired because she ____ for three hours.
p1.e: Duration up to now with a visible result: Present Perfect Continuous, have/has been + V-ing.

p1.q: This time tomorrow, I ____ the exam.
p1.e: An action in progress at a future time uses Future Continuous: will be + V-ing.
By + a future time means completed before that deadline: Future Perfect, will have + V3.

p1.q: By June, she ____ for five years.
p1.e: Duration continuing up to a future point: Future Perfect Continuous, will have been + V-ing.

o: I am seeing him last year.
I have seen him last year.
p1.e: Finished time words such as last year or yesterday are not normally used with Present Perfect. Use Past Simple.

p1.q: Does she ____ to school by bus?
p1.e: After does/doesn't/did/didn't, always use V1 (base form).

p2.e: Everyone is a singular word, so it takes a singular verb.
Each is singular: each student has.

p2.q: The list of students ____ on the desk.
p2.e: The main subject is list. The phrase of students does not change it.
Neither is singular, so use is.

p2.q: There ____ many books on the shelf.
p2.e: After there, the verb agrees with the noun that follows: many books is plural.

p2.q: My friend and my neighbour ____ teachers.
p2.e: Two subjects joined by and are plural, so use are.
News is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
Nobody is singular, so the Present Simple verb takes -s.

p2.q: One of my students ____ absent today.
p2.e: The subject is one, which is singular, not students.

p2.q: The teacher, along with his students, ____ visiting the museum.
p2.e: Along with does not make the subject plural. The main subject is teacher, so use is.
Names of subjects such as mathematics take a singular verb.

p2.q: Either the teacher or the students ____ responsible.
p2.e: With either...or, the verb agrees with the noun nearest to it. Students is plural.

p10.e: A general truth uses Zero Conditional: if + present, present.

p10.q: If I study, I ____ the exam.
p10.e: A real, possible future uses First Conditional: if + present, will + V1.

p10.q: If I ____ more time, I would study more.
p10.e: An unreal present situation uses Second Conditional: if + past, would + V1.

p10.q: If she had studied, she ____ the test.
p10.e: An unreal past uses Third Conditional: if + had + V3, would have + V3.

p10.q: If I ____ you, I would study harder.
p10.e: In the formal second conditional, use were for all subjects: If I were you.
Unless means if not. Unless you study = If you don't study, so the result clause needs a verb such as may fail.

p10.q: If it rains tomorrow, we ____ at home.
p10.e: Rain tomorrow is a real possibility, so use First Conditional with will + V1.

p10.q: If I had studied, I ____ the answer now.
p10.e: Mixed conditional: if + had + V3 (past condition), would + V1 (present result).

o: If I would study, I will pass.
If I studied, I will pass.
If I will study, I will pass.
If I study, I will pass.
p10.e: Do not normally put will directly after if in the first conditional.

p10.q: If you mix red and blue, you ____ purple.
p10.e: This is a general truth, so Zero Conditional: both clauses in the present.

p10.q: If I ____ rich, I would travel the world.
p10.e: Unreal present: Second Conditional. The formal form is if I were.

p10.q: If the students ____ harder, they would have passed.
p10.e: Third Conditional needs if + had + V3 in the if clause.

p11.e: Passive = form of BE + V3. Present Simple passive: is/are + V3.
Yesterday means past; the letter receives the action: was + V3.
Present Continuous passive: am/is/are + being + V3.
Present Perfect passive: have/has been + V3. Already supports the perfect tense.

p11.q: The students ____ by the teacher when the bell rang.
p11.e: Past Continuous passive: was/were + being + V3, for an action in progress in the past.

p11.q: They taught English. Which is the passive version?
p11.e: Preserve the tense: Past Simple taught becomes was taught.

p11.q: The books ____ by the students last week.
p11.e: Last week is past and the books receive the action: were + V3.
In a passive sentence the subject receives the action: be + V3 (here is being written).

p11.q: The project ____ when the manager arrived.
p11.e: Finished before another past action: Past Perfect passive, had been + V3.

p11.q: The core passive formula is the right form of BE + ____.
p11.e: The main verb is always in V3 (past participle). Change only the form of be to match the tense.

p19.e: Third person singular in Present Simple takes -s: he goes.
Use does + V1 with she/he/it, and do not add -s to the main verb.
After did, use V1: Did you go?
Agree is already a verb, so do not add am.
The correct preposition is married to.
Discuss takes a direct object; do not add about.
Information is uncountable. Use much, some or a lot of, not many.

p19.q: She has lived here ____ five years.
p19.e: For is used with a duration; since is used with a starting point.
After a modal, use V1 and never add -s.

p19.q: If I ____ time tomorrow, I will call you.
p19.e: In the first conditional, do not put will in the if clause.
In look forward to, to is a preposition, so use -ing.
Information and advice are uncountable: no plural and no a/an.

p9.q: You ____ follow the school rules. It is compulsory.
p9.e: Must expresses strong obligation. Might and may express weaker possibility or permission.
Core rule: modal + V1. Never add -s after a modal and never add to.

p9.q: ____ you help me with this exercise, please?
p9.e: Could is used for polite requests. Must and should do not make requests.

p9.q: It ____ rain this afternoon, but I am not sure.
p9.e: Might expresses weaker possibility, which fits I am not sure.

p9.q: The ground is wet, so it ____ last night.
p9.e: Must have + V3 shows a strong conclusion about the past.

p9.q: You ____ harder. Now you have failed the test.
p9.e: Should have + V3 expresses past advice or regret.

p9.q: I ____ to the concert, but I had no ticket.
p9.e: Could have + V3 expresses a past possibility or missed opportunity.

p9.q: We ____ wear a uniform at our school; it is the school's rule.
p9.e: Have to expresses external obligation: the rule comes from outside the speaker.

p9.q: Teachers ____ to be patient with their students.
p9.e: Ought to expresses advice or duty. It is the only one of these that is followed by to.
May is used to ask for permission.

o: You must to follow the rules.
p9.e: A modal is followed directly by V1: no to, no -s, no -ing.

p9.q: Which meaning does should usually express?
p9.e: Should is used for advice and expectation. External obligation is have to; a promise is will.

p12.q: "I like English," she said. She said that she ____ English.
p12.e: Present Simple changes to Past Simple in reported speech.

p12.q: "I am studying," he said. He said that he ____.
p12.e: Present Continuous changes to Past Continuous.

p12.q: "I have finished," she said. She said that she ____.
p12.e: Present Perfect changes to Past Perfect.

p12.q: "I visited the museum," he said. He said that he ____ the museum.
p12.e: Past Simple usually changes to Past Perfect.

p12.q: "I will help you," she said. She said that she ____ help me.
p12.e: Will changes to would in reported speech.

p12.q: "I can swim," he said. He said that he ____ swim.
"I may come," she said. She said that she ____ come.
p12.e: May changes to might in reported speech.

p12.q: "We will leave tomorrow," they said. They said they would leave ____.
p12.e: Tomorrow changes to the next day.

p12.q: In reported speech, now usually changes to ____.
p12.e: Now becomes then. Here becomes there.

p12.q: "Where do you live?" she asked me. She asked me ____.
p12.e: A reported question uses statement order, not question order, and the tense moves back.

p12.q: "Study hard," the teacher said. The teacher told us ____.
p12.e: Commands are reported with tell/told + object + to + V1.

p12.q: Past Simple in direct speech usually becomes ____ in reported speech.
p12.e: The tense moves one step back: Past Simple becomes Past Perfect.

p3.e: Article choice depends on sound. Honest starts with a vowel sound because the h is silent.

p3.q: She studies at ____ university in the city.
p3.e: University begins with a consonant sound (/j/), so use a.
Use the for something unique: there is only one sun.

p3.q: Sokha is ____ best student in the class.
In general, ____ students need regular practice.
p3.e: A general plural noun takes the zero article.

p3.q: I believe that ____ education is important for every country.
p3.e: Education is used in a general sense, so it takes the zero article.

p3.q: I saw an accident yesterday. ____ accident was very serious.
p3.e: The accident is now specific and already mentioned, so use the.
Hour begins with a vowel sound (silent h), so use an.

o: She is the a university student.
p3.e: University begins with a consonant sound, so the article is a.

p3.q: Can you pass me ____ book on the table?
p3.e: Use the for a specific, known thing: the book on the table.
Engineer begins with a vowel sound, so use an.
Information is uncountable: no a/an and no plural.

p8.e: Use on for days and dates.
Use in for months, years and long periods.
Since is used with a starting point.

p8.q: He has taught English ____ ten years.
p8.e: For is used with a duration.
By shows a deadline: not later than Friday.

p8.q: I will stay in the library ____ five o'clock.
p8.e: Until shows that an action continues up to a time.
During is used for something within a period or event.
Despite (or in spite of) is followed by a noun or -ing. Although needs a clause.

p8.q: He was late ____ the heavy traffic.
p8.e: Because of is followed by a noun or -ing; because needs a clause.

p8.q: The prize was shared ____ the three winners.
p8.e: Among is used for a group of three or more; between is for two.

p8.q: The ball is ____ the two boxes.

p13.e: Decide is followed by to + V1.

p13.q: We are interested in ____ new methods.
The teacher made the students ____ the dialogue.
p13.e: Make + object + V1, with no to.

p13.q: She asked me ____ her with the homework.
I look forward to ____ you next week.
p13.e: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so use -ing.
Hope is followed by to + V1.

p13.q: Find the error: She (A) refused (B) answering (C) the question (D) politely.
p13.e: Refuse is followed by to + V1: She refused to answer the question politely.

p13.q: Find the error: They (A) let (B) the students (C) to leave (D) early.
p13.e: Let + object + V1, with no to: They let the students leave early.

p13.q: Find the error: She is (A) interested in (B) to learn (C) new teaching methods (D) this year.
p13.e: After a preposition, use -ing: interested in learning.

p14.q: The teacher ____ helped me was kind.
The book ____ I bought is useful.
The student ____ book was lost is absent.
The school ____ I studied is nearby.
The year ____ I graduated was important.

o: My teacher who, lives nearby is helpful.
My teacher, who lives nearby, is helpful.
My teacher, that lives nearby, is helpful.
My teacher, whose lives nearby, is helpful.
p14.e: Do not use that in a non-defining clause (the one with commas). Use who.

p14.q: The teacher ____ I met was helpful.
p14.e: Whom is used for people as the object, in formal English.

p14.q: The book ____ is on the table belongs to me.
p14.e: That can be used for things in a defining clause.

p14.q: She is the student ____ won the prize.
p14.e: Who is the subject for a person.

p14.q: Find the error: The teacher (A) whose (B) I met (C) yesterday (D) was very helpful.
p14.e: Whose shows possession. For a person as object, use whom, who or that: The teacher whom I met.

p14.q: Find the error: My brother, (A) that (B) lives in the city, (C) is (D) a teacher.
p14.e: A clause between commas is non-defining, so do not use that. Use who: My brother, who lives in the city, is a teacher.

p14.q: Find the error: The year (A) where (B) I graduated (C) was (D) important.
p14.e: Where is for places. For time, use when: The year when I graduated.

p7.q: This room is ____ than that one.
p7.e: Short adjectives add -er in the comparative.

p7.q: This book is ____ than that one.
p7.e: Long adjectives use more + adjective in the comparative.

p7.q: She is the ____ student in the class.
p7.e: Short adjectives add -est in the superlative, with the.

p7.q: This is the ____ interesting lesson of the course.
p7.e: Long adjectives use the most + adjective in the superlative.
Good is irregular: good, better, best.

p7.q: This exam was ____ than the last one.
p7.e: Bad is irregular: bad, worse, worst.

p7.q: He is as tall ____ his brother.
The test was ____ as difficult as I expected.
p7.e: Negative equality: not as + adjective + as.
Much is irregular: much, more, most. Use more with than.

p7.q: Find the error: This is (A) the more (B) important lesson (C) in the (D) whole course.
p7.e: Use the superlative with in the whole course: the most important lesson.

p7.q: Find the error: She is (A) more smarter (B) than (C) her (D) sister.
p7.e: Do not use more with an -er adjective. Use smarter only.

p7.q: Find the error: My English is (A) not as (B) good (C) than (D) yours.
p7.e: Equality uses as ... as, not than: not as good as yours.

p15.q: He was tired ____ he went to bed early.
____ it was raining, we played football.
p15.e: Although is followed by a clause (subject + verb).
Despite is followed by a noun or -ing.

p15.q: She stayed home ____ she was ill.
p15.e: Because is followed by a clause.
Because of is followed by a noun or -ing.

p15.q: I studied hard ____ I could pass the exam.
The first group worked hard. ____, the second group did not.
p15.e: However shows contrast between two sentences.

p15.q: He missed the bus. ____, he arrived late.
p15.e: As a result introduces a result.

p15.q: Find the error: (A) Despite (B) it was raining, (C) we continued (D) the lesson.
p15.e: Despite needs a noun or -ing. Use Although it was raining, or Despite the rain.

p15.q: Find the error: He was absent (A) because of (B) he was sick (C) yesterday (D) morning.
p15.e: Because of is followed by a noun or -ing. Before a clause, use because.

p15.q: Find the error: (A) Although (B) she was tired, (C) but she (D) continued working.
p15.e: Do not use but together with although. One conjunction is enough: Although she was tired, she continued working.

p4.e: Advice is uncountable: some advice, a piece of advice.

p4.q: She gave us a lot of ____.
p4.e: Information is uncountable and has no plural.

p4.q: There are ____ students in the room.
p4.e: Use many with countable plural nouns.

p4.q: He does not have ____ information about the test.
There are ____ students today than yesterday.
p4.e: Use fewer with countable nouns: fewer students.

p4.q: We have ____ time than we thought.
p4.e: Use less with uncountable nouns: less time.
Homework is uncountable. You cannot say a homework or homeworks.

o: She gave me a piece of advice.
p4.e: Advice is uncountable, so use a piece of advice or some advice.
Equipment is uncountable and has no plural.

p4.q: Find the error: She (A) gave (B) me (C) many informations (D) yesterday.
p4.e: Information is uncountable: much information, not many informations.

p4.q: Find the error: He (A) asked me (B) for an advice (C) about (D) the exam.
p4.e: Advice is uncountable: for some advice or for a piece of advice.

p4.q: Find the error: (A) Fewer (B) information (C) is (D) available online.
p4.e: Information is uncountable, so use less information, not fewer.

p5.e: A subject pronoun is needed before the verb: she.
After a verb, use an object pronoun: me.

p5.q: This is my book. That one is ____.
p5.e: A possessive pronoun stands alone with no noun after it: yours.
A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and object are the same person.
Its shows possession. It's means it is or it has.
It's = it is. Its is for possession.
Those is the plural demonstrative for things or people that are far.
A possessive adjective comes before a noun: their homework.

p5.q: The pen on the desk is ____.
p5.e: A possessive pronoun replaces a noun: theirs.

p5.q: Find the error: (A) Her (B) and I (C) went (D) to the library.
p5.e: Use a subject pronoun: She and I went to the library.

p5.q: Find the error: The dog wagged (A) it's (B) tail (C) when (D) it saw me.
p5.e: It's means it is. For possession, use its: The dog wagged its tail.

p5.q: Find the error: He (A) hurt (B) him (C) while he (D) was cooking.
p5.e: When the subject and object are the same person, use a reflexive pronoun: himself.

p6.e: An adjective describes a noun: a careful teacher.
An adverb describes a verb: works carefully.
Well is the adverb that describes how he speaks.
Good is the adjective that describes a noun.
Hard means with effort. Hardly means almost not.
Hardly means almost not: he could almost not believe it.
Lately means recently. Late means not early.
Nearly means almost. Near means close.

p6.q: Find the error: She (A) speaks (B) English (C) very (D) good.
p6.e: Speaks is a verb, so use the adverb well: very well.

p6.q: Find the error: He (A) works (B) very hardly (C) every (D) day.
p6.e: Hardly means almost not. Use hard for effort: works very hard.

p6.q: Find the error: The teacher (A) explained (B) the lesson (C) clear (D) to us.
p6.e: An adverb describes how she explained: clearly.

p16.e: Present Simple questions with she use Does + S + V1.
Past Simple questions use Did + S + V1.
Present Continuous questions use Am/Is/Are + S + V-ing.
Present Perfect questions use Have/Has + S + V3. Have goes with you.

p16.q: ____ the class started before you arrived?
p16.e: Past Perfect questions use Had + S + V3.
Future questions use Will + S + V1.
In a subject question, who is the subject, so do/does/did is not needed.
After did, use V1: Did he go?

p16.q: Find the error: (A) Does (B) she (C) teaches (D) English?
p16.e: After does, use V1: Does she teach English?

p16.q: Find the error: (A) Where (B) did (C) you went (D) yesterday?
p16.e: After did, use V1: Where did you go yesterday?

p16.q: Find the error: (A) Who (B) does (C) teach (D) English in this school?
p16.e: Who is the subject here, so no does is needed: Who teaches English in this school?

p17.e: A positive statement takes a negative tag. Are → aren't.
A negative statement takes a positive tag. Doesn't → does.
Past Simple takes did/didn't in the tag: went → didn't they.
Repeat the modal in the tag: can → can't he.
Let's takes the tag shall we.
A command takes the tag will you.
After I am, the tag is aren't I.
Present Simple plural subject: help → don't they.
Repeat the auxiliary has in the tag: hasn't she.

p17.q: Find the error: He (A) likes (B) coffee, (C) isn't (D) he?
p17.e: Present Simple with he: likes → doesn't he.

p17.q: Find the error: They (A) don't (B) work (C) here, (D) don't they?
p17.e: A negative statement takes a positive tag: do they.

p17.q: Find the error: Let's (A) go (B) now, (C) will (D) we?
p17.e: Let's takes shall we, not will we.

p18.q: Students study. What type of sentence is this?
Students study, and teachers help. What type is this?
p18.e: Two independent clauses joined by and: compound.

p18.q: Students study because they want to improve. What type is this?
p18.e: An independent clause plus a dependent clause starting with because: complex.

p18.q: Students study, and teachers help because the exam is important. What type is this?
p18.e: Two independent clauses plus a dependent clause: compound-complex.

o: She stayed home because she was ill.
She was tired, but she studied, and she passed.
She was ill, so she stayed home.
p18.e: Only the first has an independent clause plus a dependent clause (because she was ill).

o: two independent clauses and a conjunction
one independent clause and at least one dependent clause
an independent clause and a dependent clause
two independent clauses with a conjunction
p18.e: Compound = two or more independent clauses joined by a conjunction.

p18.q: Which list shows the FANBOYS conjunctions?
o: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
p18.e: FANBOYS = for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

p18.q: Which word is a FANBOYS conjunction?
p18.e: Yet is a FANBOYS word. The others begin dependent clauses.

p18.q: She studied hard, ____ she passed the exam.
p18.e: So is a FANBOYS conjunction that joins two independent clauses and shows a result.

o: Students study, and teachers help because the exam is important.
Teachers help students, and students learn.
Students study because they want to improve.
Students study, and teachers help because the exam is important.
p18.e: Two independent clauses plus a dependent clause: compound-complex.

irregular.q: What is the past simple of go?

irregular.e: Present Perfect needs V3: write – wrote – written.
See – saw – seen. Last week needs Past Simple: saw.
Eat – ate – eaten. Have needs V3.
Sing – sang – sung. Past Simple uses sang.

irregular.q: Which line is correct (V1 – V2 – V3)?
Find the error: She (A) has (B) wrote (C) three (D) essays this week.
Find the error: He (A) buyed (B) a new book (C) last (D) week.
irregular.e: Buy – bought – bought: He bought a new book.

irregular.q: Find the error: They have (A) went (B) to the market (C) and (D) bought fruit.
irregular.e: Have needs V3 of go: have gone.
